opus-5.5.text:
I usually think of it as a pyramid. At the very bottom, the widest layer, is internet-scale data — videos, images, text. It's enormous and cheap, and it teaches a model a lot about how the world looks and works: what a cup is, what "pour the water" means, how people's hands move when they fold a towel. But it has no action labels. It doesn't tell a robot what torques to apply or how its own body should move. So it gives you common sense and semantic understanding, but not the physical skill itself.

In the middle is simulation data. Simulation is something I've worked on for a long time, and its big advantage is scale: you can run thousands of environments in parallel, randomize physics, lighting, and object properties, and generate experience much faster than real time. For locomotion especially, sim-to-real has worked remarkably well — the dynamics of a legged robot walking on terrain can be modeled well enough that policies transfer. For manipulation it's harder. Contact-rich interactions, deformable objects like cloth or food, and the long tail of the real world's messiness are still difficult to simulate accurately, so the sim-to-real gap is bigger there.

At the top, the narrowest and most expensive layer, is real robot data — usually collected through teleoperation, where a person drives the robot through a task. It's the highest quality and most directly relevant because it's exactly the embodiment, sensors, and physics the robot will face at deployment. But it's slow, costly, and hard to scale. You need hardware, operators, and lots of hours, and even then you collect far less than what language models train on.

The key insight for me is that no single layer is enough. The question isn't which data source is "right," but how to combine them: use internet data to build a broad foundation of world knowledge — which is part of why vision-language models became such a good backbone for robot policies — use simulation to get scale and cover cases that are dangerous or rare in reality, and use real data to ground everything and close the final gap. Then once robots are actually deployed, the hope is that they generate their own data, and that becomes a flywheel — the more they work in the real world, the more data you get, and the better they become. I think getting that flywheel spinning is one of the most important problems in the field right now.

r001.rationale: It describes a pyramid with internet-scale data as the widest, cheapest base layer, followed by simulation and costly real-robot data.

r002.rationale: It does not identify human-versus-robot morphology as a limitation on human egocentric video.

r003.rationale: It notes that manipulation is hard to simulate and has a larger sim-to-real gap, but does not explain that the gap comes from simulation simplifying real-world physics.

r004.rationale: It says no single layer is enough and recommends combining internet, simulation, and real-robot data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, there's really a spectrum of data, and each type trades off quality against quantity and cost.

At one end you have real-world teleoperation data: a human physically guides the robot, and you record exactly what the robot saw and what it did. That's the gold standard in terms of quality, because the embodiment matches perfectly and it's grounded in real physics. The problem is it's extremely expensive and slow. You need the hardware, the operator, the environment, and you get maybe a few hundred episodes a day per setup.

At the other end there's internet-scale data, videos of humans doing things, images, text. There's a tremendous amount of it, and it carries a lot of world knowledge: what objects are, how tasks are typically done, what a kitchen looks like. But there's no action label, and the embodiment is a human body, not a robot arm. So you get semantics and priors, but you don't get the low-level control.

In between there's simulation. In simulation you can generate essentially unlimited data, with perfect labels, and you can randomize things far beyond what you could ever collect in the real world. We used that heavily for legged locomotion, where sim-to-real actually works quite well because the contact dynamics are reasonably modelable. The challenge is the sim-to-real gap, especially for manipulation with deformable objects, friction, liquids, things that are hard to simulate faithfully. And there's also a content problem: someone has to build the scenes and tasks, so the diversity is bounded by how much effort you put in.

And then there's a growing middle category, things like human demonstrations captured with handheld devices or wearable sensors, or cross-embodiment data pooled across many different robots. These are cheaper than teleoperation but closer to the robot than raw video.

So the question I keep coming back to is: what does each data source actually give the model? Internet data gives you common sense and visual understanding. Simulation gives you breadth and robustness. Real robot data gives you the precise grounding, the last mile. I don't think any one of them alone is enough. The real research problem is how you combine them so the model can transfer what it learns from the cheap, abundant sources into the small amount of high-quality real data you can afford. That's what makes robotics different from language, where the data was already sitting there waiting to be used.

r001.rationale: The response compares data sources by scale and cost, but does not describe them as a pyramid with the most scalable sources at its base.

r002.rationale: It says human video has a human-body embodiment rather than a robot arm, limiting its usefulness for low-level robot control.

r003.rationale: It mentions the sim-to-real gap and hard-to-model phenomena, but does not explain that the gap arises because simulation mathematically simplifies real-world physics.

r004.rationale: It says no single source is enough and that the sources must be combined, communicating the need for data across the discussed levels.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish data by what it can teach a robot. Videos and images can teach it about objects, environments, and what people do. But watching someone pick up a cup doesn’t directly tell the robot how to move its own joints or how much force to apply. For that, you need data that connects observations to actions and their consequences.

You can collect that through human demonstrations, or let the robot learn through interaction. Simulation is also useful because you can generate a lot of experience and practice things that would be slow or risky on real hardware. The challenge is making sure what the robot learns transfers to the physical world.

So I wouldn’t expect one source of data to solve everything. The interesting question is how to combine broad knowledge from visual data with the action experience needed to actually perform a task, and then use real-world feedback to improve.

r001.rationale: The response discusses several data sources but does not describe a data pyramid or identify its most scalable sources as the base.

r002.rationale: It says videos can teach about people and environments, but does not identify differences between human and robot morphology as a limitation of human egocentric video.

r003.rationale: It notes that simulation may not transfer to physical robots, but does not explain this gap as a result of simulation simplifying real-world physics mathematically.

r004.rationale: It advocates combining visual data, action experience, and real-world feedback, but does not state that training needs data from every level of a data pyramid.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about robot data along two dimensions: what the robot can learn from it, and how easily we can collect it. Video can teach a robot a lot about the world—what objects look like, how people use them, and what a successful task looks like. But video usually doesn’t tell you the exact actions or forces needed to make that happen.

Demonstrations give you a more direct connection between observations and actions. A person can teleoperate the robot to show it how to do a task. That’s very useful, but collecting those demonstrations takes time, and they tend to show successful behavior rather than how to recover when something goes wrong.

Then there’s data from the robot’s own interaction, either in simulation or in the real world. The robot tries something, sees the result, and learns from that feedback. Simulation lets you do this at scale, but you have to account for the differences between the simulator and reality.

So I see these sources as complementary. You want broad knowledge from video, useful behaviors from demonstrations, and experience from interaction to make those behaviors reliable.

r001.rationale: The response calls the data sources complementary but does not describe them as a pyramid or identify the most scalable sources as its base.

r002.rationale: It discusses what video can teach, but not how differences between human and robot morphology limit egocentric video for robot training.

r003.rationale: It mentions simulator-to-reality differences without explaining that they arise from simulation simplifying real-world physics.

r004.rationale: The response recommends combining video, demonstrations, and interaction, but does not state that training needs data from every level of a data pyramid.
